newsitem.title: USA: Credit card delinquencies slow in third quarter.
newsitem.headline: Credit card delinquencies slow in third quarter.

text.p: High-flying consumers, flashing credit cards at retailers like so many Saracen swords, may be showing a bit more caution, the American Bankers Association reported Wednesday.

Late payments on credit cards dropped to a seasonally adjusted 3.48 percent in this year's third quarter from an all-time high of 3.66 percent in the second three months. It was the first decrease in two years, the ABA said.

"We hope that the drop is a sign that consumers are taking control of their finances, rather than just taking a quick break before hitting the next holiday sale," said James Chessen, chief economist of the ABA.
The new data, if it becomes a trend, is a breath of fresh air for a consumer credit situation that has troubled banks, Federal regulators and credit card companies.
Banks, for their part, appear to be showing restraint after years of bombarding consumers with credit card offers.

This comes as Americans are declaring bankruptcy, the last destination of the imprudent consumer, at record levels. Bankruptcy filings were up 26 percent to 1.11 million for the judicial year ended Sept. 30.

Federal Reserve Governor Lawrence Lindsey, a major critic of the buildup in debt, has made clear that it is unsustainable and some economists have worried that a slowing economy will make it much worse.
Speaking earlier this month at a conference sponsored by the Consumer Federation of America, Lindsey said that roughly for every extra $1 Americans earn, they spend $1.10.
"In the period ahead, I think that high and perhaps rising levels of consumer debt will actually cause the bankruptcy rate to rise further," he said.
The credit card companies think it should be harder to declare bankruptcy, saying it is just too easy for Americans to walk away from their debt and start over.

"Today's consumer bankruptcy system unnecessarily harms consumers and creditors alike because of a fundamental flaw -- it allows debtors to discharge debts even if the debtors can repay some or all of those debts," a coalition of banks and credit card companies said Tuesday.
The coalition spoke at a hearing of the congressionally mandated National Bankruptcy Review Commission, which is to report next October on recommendations for changing the current bankruptcy laws.
The ABA's latest report said the slowing economy was a factor in the decline in delinquencies. In its sixth year of expansion, the economy has leveled off from stronger growth earlier this year.

"Slowed consumer spending in the third quarter along with banks' efforts to tighten credit standards and charge off problem consumer loans combined to bring the late payments down," said ABA's Chessen.
The economy, which grew by a moderate 2.0 percent in the third quarter, is expected to strengthen slightly this year and keep at about that pace in 1997.
But if it does worse than expected, the debt load being carried by the consumer may become too much to bear, tempting more people to use the bankruptcy option.
"Debt loads are never a big problem when the economy is strong or rising, but when it stumbles into recession, it can become a big problem," said David Jones, economist at Aubrey G. Lanston.
